title: 5 important ways in which learning is helped by a shared agreement about the kinds of people we are helping our children and students to become.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton continues his series on factors affecting learning with five ways a shared agreement about the kinds of people a school is helping children become supports learning. First, it shapes the curriculum's outcomes, repeated experiences and assessments, which he illustrates with Dickens's Fagin and his own curriculum-development work. Second, it justifies why things are done, giving a consistent answer to the constant debate that surrounds schools. Third, it helps parents choose a school and gives later conversations a framework. Fourth, it builds community at the level of big ideas rather than disputes over practice. Fifth, it builds consistency in curriculum, behaviour and recruitment. He ends with a six-question checklist for schools.
points: The kind of person a school wants to develop should drive the curriculum, since outcomes, experiences and assessments flow from it, as Fagin's effective teaching shows that good learning toward bad ends is still possible.
Values give a school a principled, repeatable way to answer constant parental and staff debate, reducing the noise that reaches students.
Telling parents plainly who the school aims to help children become lets them choose with confidence and supplies a framework if problems arise later.
Community forms around big ideas, and nobody tells a school they do not want their children to get better, so learning plus the vision builds shared meaning.
The same shared statement can anchor recruitment, job descriptions and behavioural consistency across the school.
quotes: Fagin, the pimp and thief from Charles Dickens’ Oliver Twist, was a good teacher. He helped his students learn well.

This is why schools and parents need to think about and make explicit the kinds of people we want our children and students to become. Doing so is the forerunner to deciding, like Fagin, which learning outcomes should be in our curriculum, which should matter most, which repeated experiences children and students should have and how we assess or evaluate whether they are steadily moving towards achieving the necessary outcomes.

It’s not that everyone will like the answers. They won’t. But, in my experience, answers are more likely to be respected and accepted when the questioner can see that they are thought-through and connected to a set of values that pervades the whole school and isn’t driven issue by issue.

It has often seemed to me that alongside house buying, finding a school for our child is the most important thing we do to which we give least time. A few conversations with the neighbours if we already live locally, a visit to the Head with a whistle stop tour of the school and then it’s decision time.
Community is most likely to be developed at the level of big ideas. I don’t like Taylor Swift because of her individual tracks; I hardly know them.

Literally, no-one in hundreds of meetings with parents in my own schools and schools all over the world, has yet said to me they’ve don’t want their children to get better. By focusing on learning, schools can create a shared sense of meaning for their community which cuts down on what can seem decisive, noisy and counter-productive discussions about practice.

Consistency is built better when everyone knows what kinds of children and students we want to help develop. We have seen how such a shared agreement enables curriculum consistency and how it can help communities come together.
